svg.title: Two ways a SQL validator returns a clean pass on something you did not want
svg.desc: Two panels side by side, laid out identically so the two verdicts sit at the same height. The left panel, Case A, holds a statement selecting every email address and full name from the users table with a limit of one thousand rows. All six checks are ticked in the order they run: one statement only, the root is a Select, no mutation node below the root, no SELECT INTO, no name from the sixteen-entry blocklist, and a LIMIT present and within the ceiling. The verdict is Allowed, one thousand rows and two columns, described as a thousand rows of personally identifiable information. Its caption says nothing here is a bug, because the validator has no concept of sensitive and this is indistinguishable from legitimate analytics, so column policy is a database concern. The right panel, Case B, holds an anonymous DO block that calls pg_sleep for thirty seconds. sqlglot does not raise on it: it logs to standard error that it is falling back to parsing as a Command, and the resulting walk contains only a Command node and a string Literal. Three flat dashes, deliberately not ticks, mark that there is no function node, no delete node and no limit node, so the three checks that read the tree ran, found nothing and returned cleanly. Two endings sit side by side at the same height as the left panel's verdict: the blocklist, which holds pg_sleep and saw nothing, and this server, which refuses any opaque command node on sight. Its caption says refusing an opaque node means valid PostgreSQL gets rejected, and that this is the right trade. A closing line generalizes the rule: when a parser degrades instead of failing, every check downstream of it degrades silently with it.
svg.text: Two clean passes you did not want
Left: every check ran and passed. Right: the ones that read the tree passed, having seen nothing.
Case A · every check passes
and the query is a data breach
SELECT email, full_name FROM users LIMIT 1000
one statement only
the root is a Select
no mutation node below the root
no SELECT ... INTO
no name from the 16-entry blocklist
LIMIT present, and within the ceiling
Allowed
row_count: 1000 · columns: ["email", "full_name"]
A thousand rows of personally identifiable information.
Nothing here is a bug. The validator has no concept of
"sensitive". This is indistinguishable from legitimate
analytics, and column policy is a database concern.
Case B · every content check passes
because not one of them could look inside
DO $$ BEGIN PERFORM pg_sleep(30); END $$
sqlglot does not raise. It logs to stderr and carries on:
Falling back to parsing as a 'Command'.
walk types: ['Command', 'Literal']
No Func node, no Delete node, no Limit node.
The three checks that read the tree ran,
found nothing, and returned cleanly.
The blocklist
pg_sleep is on it,
and it saw nothing.
This server
isinstance(node,
exp.Command) -> refuse
An opaque node is a node no check can see inside.
Refusing it means valid PostgreSQL gets rejected,
and that is the right trade.
When a parser degrades instead of failing, every check downstream of it degrades silently with it.
